title: The Power of Outcome Focusing
coreMove: Name the desired outcome clearly enough that actions can be tested against what done should look like.
sourcePressure: This principles chapter explains why a clear desired result gives direction to action and planning, acting as a force multiplier for lower-level control.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating outcome focusing as vision-board optimism instead of a practical standard for choosing and aligning next actions.
sourceAnchorNote: The source sidecar contains no chapter-specific named people, named studies, or named places. Use only the listed GTD terms, official metadata, or supported artifacts; do not invent anecdotes.

sourceAnchors.name: outcome focusing
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar identifies outcome focusing as the chapter’s principle-level power.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Outcome focusing gives the work a finish line that the next action can actually aim at.

sourceAnchors.name: force multiplier
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar says outcome focusing acts as a force multiplier when paired with practical workflow control.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The outcome does not do the work; it stops the work from spraying in every direction.

hook: stress is not about having too much to do
a messy desk proves the system is broken
counterintuition: the real problem is not time but attention
this is not about doing more but doing what matters
the simple move is actually the powerful one
tryThisNow: set a timer and write everything down
pick one task and make it specific
review your list and choose a priority
examples: timestamp plus name plus laptop plus decision repeated across all six examples
home kitchen clutter as mental-load shorthand

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: a discharge coordinator clearing a hospital bed before shift handover
exampleSpecs.audience: a coordinator with a patient medically cleared but not actually gone
exampleSpecs.stakes: a vague discharge item could cost another patient a bed overnight
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The printer spits out discharge papers while Emma rewrites done as signed forms, confirmed transport, and bed marked available.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: warm discharge papers sliding from a printer

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance translator reorganizing Sunday deliverables
exampleSpecs.audience: a translator managing multiple clients and versions
exampleSpecs.stakes: a brief could be returned late because the result is named only by client surname
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The apartment is quiet when Luke changes "Muller contract" into a visible finished result with final file and invoice sent.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a translation file named final beside an unsent invoice

exampleSpecs.domain: a drama teacher asking for production budget approval
exampleSpecs.audience: a teacher needing a clear result before a department head can approve spending
exampleSpecs.stakes: a budget may be bounced back because nobody can picture opening night requirements
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "What does ready look like on opening night?" Hugo’s department head asks, and the missing outcome stops the request cold.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a costume budget sheet under a stage seating chart

exampleSpecs.domain: a doctoral candidate revising a methods section before defense
exampleSpecs.audience: a researcher whose hard work is scattered by fuzzy finish conditions
exampleSpecs.stakes: a defense date could slip into another term
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 10:40 a.m., Kasia writes the outcome as methods section revised with all committee notes addressed and sent by Thursday.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a committee email printed with margin notes

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional operations manager reviewing a failed territory offsite
exampleSpecs.audience: a manager whose team spent a day moving without a defined result
exampleSpecs.stakes: the quarter plan still does not exist two weeks before it is due
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Devon one wasted offsite to see that activity had no standard because nobody named what the day had to produce.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a conference room agenda with no decision line

exampleSpecs.domain: a restaurant line cook developing a seasonal small-plates section
exampleSpecs.audience: a cook leading menu development for the first time
exampleSpecs.stakes: the chef’s deadline could arrive with attractive fragments and no finished section
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: What changes when Javier pictures the printed menu section complete before choosing tonight’s first recipe test?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a blank menu proof clipped above the prep counter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

skillTargets: use outcome to evaluate next actions
avoid replacing execution with vision language

tryThisNowSpec: For one active commitment, write a single sentence beginning "Done means" and include the visible condition that would let you stop.
